intro:
These exercises rehearse the central discipline of the chapter: name the claim each test defends, prove it at the cheapest layer that can prove it, and engineer determinism instead of hoping for it. You move from classifying which test layer fits which risk, through reading a suite to find the claims it leaves unproven, into writing property tests, planning fuzz targets for unsafe parsers, and designing async and distributed test plans that do not depend on scheduler luck.

The through-line is that an advanced Rust system fails along several independent axes at once — local invariants, hostile input, retry safety, output stability, and performance budgets — and a good suite separates those axes rather than collapsing them into one slow end-to-end lane. Every solution below commits to a concrete layer choice and justifies it in terms of cost, confidence, and the ownership or determinism property it actually exercises.

exerciseSolutions.title: Choose unit, integration, property, fuzz, snapshot, or benchmark from the claim
exerciseSolutions.solution:
Start from the claim, not the tool. The five needs are: (1) a state-machine invariant, (2) a public HTTP contract, (3) a hostile binary parser input space, (4) a large human-reviewable error report, and (5) a latency budget for one hot batch encoder. Each has a cheapest layer that can still produce the right kind of evidence, and the report (4) needs two answers — an output-review layer for its shape plus a semantic assertion for its load-bearing fields.

The state-machine invariant is a unit test first. It is a local, pure rule — a transition either rejects a duplicate submission or it does not — and you can assert it without booting a runtime, a database, or a network. Unit tests are the cheapest, most deterministic layer, so any claim that lives inside one type or one function belongs here. If the same invariant needs to hold across an unbounded space of operation sequences, you later lift it into a property test, but the first proof is a unit test.

The public HTTP contract is a true integration test, because the claim is about a public seam another deployment unit depends on. You drive the handler through a test app and assert the status code and the durable side effect, which is exactly what a downstream caller observes. A unit test cannot prove the seam composed correctly; only exercising the boundary does.

The hostile binary parser input space is fuzzing. The input is malformed by nature, the space is adversarial, and a coverage-guided fuzzer explores byte sequences no human fixture author would write. This is distinct from a property test in degree of hostility: property testing generates structured-but-random valid-ish inputs around an invariant; fuzzing pushes openly malformed bytes at a parser to find crashes, panics, and undefined behavior.

The large human-reviewable error report is a snapshot or golden review. The output is big and shaped, so a byte-for-byte committed artifact (golden file) or a review-and-accept diff (snapshot) is the practical way to detect unintended changes — provided you normalize nondeterministic fields and pair it with a semantic assertion for any load-bearing value. The latency budget for the hot batch encoder is a benchmark with a coarse budget, kept in its own lane: it proves a performance claim, not a correctness claim, and must not be mixed into the functional suite where its hardware sensitivity would cause flakes.
criteria: Maps each of the five claims to a primary layer (unit, integration, fuzz, snapshot/golden, benchmark) with a cost-and-confidence justification.
Distinguishes snapshot/golden review of output shape from semantic correctness assertions, and notes the report still needs a semantic check for load-bearing values.
Keeps the latency budget in a separate benchmark lane, explicitly out of the functional correctness suite.

exerciseSolutions.title: Find the missing layers in one test suite
exerciseSolutions.solution:
The suite is expensive and still incomplete because every claim is being proven at the most costly layer, and several claims are not being proven at all. Slow API integration tests can only show that the whole stack composed on the happy path; they say almost nothing about the local rules underneath.

Missing unit or property layers: the domain model has no direct tests, so invariants like 'quota never exceeds limit' or 'a duplicate submission is rejected' are only ever exercised incidentally through a full HTTP round-trip. Those rules should move down. The ones with a single fixed expectation become unit tests; the ones that should hold across many generated operation sequences become property tests, where the framework shrinks any failure to a minimal counterexample. Pushing them down makes them fast, deterministic, and attributable to one type rather than to a whole request.

Missing fuzz layer: the binary parser is only reached through end-to-end fixtures, which means it is tested against the handful of inputs a human thought to write. A parser is exactly the boundary where arbitrary external bytes cross into your code, so it wants a coverage-guided fuzz target on the small raw-bytes-to-parse-result function, with crashing inputs saved into a corpus as permanent regression cases. Fixtures prove a few known frames decode; fuzzing probes the malformed-input space the fixtures cannot.

Async determinism problem: the worker tests use real sleeps, so they depend on scheduler luck — they pass on a fast laptop and flake in CI. The repair is to take time out of the operating system's hands: drive a paused or fake clock, advance it explicitly past the relevant deadline, and assert the resulting state, so the test is deterministic regardless of machine speed. Finally, blindly accepting snapshot updates is too trusting for a production-facing report format: an accepted diff records 'the output changed', not 'the output is correct', so a regression can be rubber-stamped into the golden state. Snapshots should gate on human review of the diff and be paired with a semantic assertion on any load-bearing field.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: One repair per gap: property test for the domain invariant, a small fuzz boundary for the parser, and a fake-clock async test that never really sleeps.
criteria: Identifies the untested domain invariants as a missing unit/property layer, the un-fuzzed parser as a missing fuzz layer, and the sleep-based worker tests as the async determinism problem.

Proposes a concrete repair for each: lift invariants into unit/property tests, add a small raw-bytes fuzz target with a corpus, drive a paused clock instead of sleeping, and gate snapshot diffs on review plus a semantic assertion.
Explains the suite is expensive yet incomplete because all claims are pushed to the slow end-to-end layer while local invariants, hostile input, and time control go unproven.

exerciseSolutions.title: Write property tests for a domain invariant
exerciseSolutions.solution:
State the invariant before the generator. For a quota window the rule is plain: after any sequence of reservation requests, used never exceeds limit. That is a property of the type, not of a particular sequence, which is exactly why a property test fits better than a few hand-picked examples — the framework supplies the sequences and tries to break the rule.

The generator serves the invariant. It produces a random limit and a random-length vector of random quantities, so the test covers many interleavings of accepted and rejected reservations rather than the two or three a human would type. Crucially, the assertion is the invariant itself (used <= limit) evaluated after every operation, not a check against a specific expected total. A deterministic reference rule keeps the expectation honest: a reservation is accepted only when used + qty <= limit, and the test re-derives acceptance the same way the type should, so the property describes the rule the subsystem actually cares about.

When the invariant fails, shrinking is what makes the failure useful. proptest reduces the counterexample to the smallest input that still violates the rule — typically the shortest operation sequence and the smallest quantities that drive used past limit. Instead of a 30-element random vector you get something like a single oversized reservation, which points straight at the off-by-one or the missing bounds check in try_reserve. The random data on its own proves little; the minimized failing case is the payoff.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: The assertion is the invariant itself; proptest generates the sequences and shrinks any failure to the smallest violating case.
criteria: Expresses one real invariant ('used never exceeds limit after any sequence') in clear domain terms, stated before the generator.
Generates a random limit and a variable-length vector of quantities rather than a single fixed example.
Explains that on failure proptest shrinks to the minimal sequence and smallest quantities, turning a large random case into a pinpointed counterexample.

exerciseSolutions.title: Plan fuzz targets for unsafe parsing code
exerciseSolutions.solution:
Pick the smallest boundary that still reproduces a crash. The fuzz target should be the raw-bytes-to-parse-result function — bytes in, structured result or error out — not the whole transport stack. Keeping the harness close to the parser means a crashing input is a few bytes that still mean something: it points at one decoder rather than at an entire service, and it reproduces in milliseconds. A fuzz target wrapped around the full stack would waste most of its budget on framing and IO that have nothing to do with the unsafe fast path.

A day-one seed corpus should cover the structural edges the unsafe path is most likely to mishandle: an empty input, a truncated frame that ends mid-header, a frame with an exact valid header, a header whose declared length is oversized relative to the actual payload, a duplicated frame, and a malformed footer. These are the classes where a byte walker either reads past the buffer or trusts a length field it should have validated, so seeding them gives the coverage-guided fuzzer good starting points to mutate from.

Compare the unsafe fast path against a safe reference parser as a differential oracle: run both on the same bytes and assert they agree — same accept/reject decision and, on accept, the same decoded structure. Where a full reference is too costly, assert explicit structural invariants instead: the cursor never advances past the buffer length, the declared payload length is validated before the cursor walks it, and every offset derived inside the unsafe block stays in bounds. Either way you are checking the invariant edges where UB actually lives, not just that a happy-path frame decodes.

The fuzz lane must fail immediately on the signals that catch the bugs you cannot see from a passing return value. Run the target under AddressSanitizer so out-of-bounds reads and use-after-free abort the run, treat any panic or abort as a failure, and use Miri or sanitizer UB detection on the unsafe path to catch invalid pointer use and aliasing violations that an optimized build might otherwise hide. Save every crashing input into the corpus so each fix ships with a permanent regression case.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: Small raw-bytes boundary with a differential oracle against a safe reference; seed classes and sanitizer/panic signals listed alongside.
criteria: Picks the small raw-bytes-to-result function as the fuzz boundary and justifies it (crashing inputs stay meaningful and reproduce fast).
Defines at least five seed classes: empty, truncated, exact header, oversized length, duplicated frame, malformed footer.
Specifies a differential oracle against a safe reference parser, plus explicit unsafe invariants (cursor in bounds, length validated before walk) when a full reference is too costly.
Includes failing tool signals: AddressSanitizer aborts, any panic/abort, and Miri/UB detection, with crashes saved to the corpus.

exerciseSolutions.title: Design async integration tests for a service boundary
exerciseSolutions.solution:
The pipeline is HTTP request to async worker to database write to queue publish, and the safety claim is that the retry path stays idempotent under duplicate delivery or cancellation. The plan makes time, durable effects, task joins, and identity explicit instead of leaving them to scheduler luck.

Fake time goes wherever the test would otherwise wait. The retry backoff and any lease or timeout deadline run on a paused runtime (Tokio's start_paused), and the test advances the clock explicitly past each deadline rather than sleeping. That makes the retry behavior deterministic: the same advance sequence drives the same redelivery every run, on any machine. If the plan still calls a real sleep, it is not deterministic enough.

The durable side effects must be asserted before the handler is considered done, and at the durable boundary, not at the HTTP status. The test asserts the database write landed exactly once and the outbox or queue contains exactly one publish for the request — checking the store and the outbox directly. A 200 status only proves the request was accepted; the side-effect assertions prove the work actually crossed the seam and crossed it once.

Idempotency is the load-bearing assertion: deliver the same message ID twice and assert the durable effect happened exactly once, because the worker consults a completion record keyed by that ID before applying the effect. The test separates three failure modes that look similar from the outside — a join failure (the spawned task panicked or was aborted, surfaced by the JoinHandle as a JoinError, distinguishing panic from cancellation), an inner failure (the task ran and returned a domain Err), and cancellation (the task was dropped before completing). Asserting on the JoinHandle result distinguishes join-level outcomes from the inner operation's Result. Throughout, the assertions carry identity fields — the request ID, the task or message ID, and the idempotency key written to the outbox row — so that when a case fails later it stays attributable to a specific message rather than to 'something in the worker'.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: Paused runtime drives retries deterministically; assertions land at the db and outbox boundary, keyed by message id, with join vs inner vs cancellation separated.
criteria: Uses a deterministic time-control technique (start_paused plus explicit advance) for retry/backoff deadlines instead of real sleeps.
Defines an idempotency assertion at the durable boundary: the same message id delivered twice yields exactly one db write and one outbox publish.
Separates task-join behavior (JoinError, cancelled vs panicked) from the inner operation's Result.
Describes what happens to in-flight work under cancellation (the task dropped before completing) as distinct from a panic or a typed inner error.
Carries identity fields (request id, message id, idempotency key) into the assertions so failures stay attributable.

exerciseSolutions.title: Build a production test matrix for a distributed Rust subsystem
exerciseSolutions.solution:
The service parses binary frames, enriches them asynchronously, writes an outbox entry, renders operator reports, and exposes an FFI plugin boundary. The matrix proves different claims at different costs and keeps the end-to-end lane narrow.

Unit and property layer. Local domain invariants stay here: enrichment rules, outbox state transitions, and any 'never exceeds / always rejects duplicate' rule. Single-expectation rules are unit tests; rules that must hold across many generated sequences become property tests so failures shrink to minimal counterexamples. This is the cheapest, most deterministic layer and most claims should live here.

Fuzz and unsafe-invariant layer. The binary frame parser gets a coverage-guided fuzz target on the small raw-bytes-to-result function, with a seed corpus (empty, truncated, exact header, oversized length, duplicated frame, malformed footer) and crashes saved as regressions. The FFI plugin boundary gets unsafe-invariant tests run under Miri and a sanitizer, because a UB bug there may not be observable from a passing return value. This layer proves hostile-input and unsafe-edge handling that fixtures cannot.

Output-review layer. The operator report — large, shaped, human-reviewed — uses a snapshot (insta-style accept/reject diff) for shape, gated on review and paired with a semantic assertion on load-bearing fields. The wire frame the service emits, an external byte-for-byte contract, uses a golden file with nondeterministic fields (timestamps, UUIDs) normalized before comparison. Golden for the strict external contract, snapshot for the reviewable human report.

Performance-regression layer. The hot encoder or enrichment path gets a benchmark guarded by a single coarse budget (for example p95 <= 250 microseconds), marked #[ignore] so it stays out of the correctness run, and executed in a separate performance lane on stable hardware. It is looser and isolated because it is hardware-sensitive and guards a budget, not a value. Finally, the minimum end-to-end suite is one or two happy-path flows — request in, enrich, outbox row written, publish observed at the durable boundary, asserted on identity (message id, idempotency key), with retries driven by a paused clock. That narrow lane proves the transport reality composed without turning CI into a random-timing lottery; every sharper claim has already been proven more cheaply below it.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: Five lanes, each proving one kind of claim at its cheapest layer; the end-to-end lane is deliberately narrow.
criteria: Defines at least four distinct lanes: unit/property, fuzz/unsafe, output review, performance regression, plus a narrow end-to-end lane.
Includes one property/invariant layer, one fuzz/unsafe layer, one output-review layer (golden and snapshot), and one isolated performance-regression layer.
Justifies each lane by the claim it proves and why it sits at that cost level.
Keeps the end-to-end lane to one or two happy-path flows asserted at the durable boundary on identity, avoiding a random-timing CI lottery.

labSolution.explanation:
The lab completes the harness by fixing the broken reservation method. The starter's `reserve` unconditionally added `qty` and returned `true`, which could push `used` past `limit` and would make the invariant report a violation. The solution replaces it with `try_reserve`, the chapter's checked version: it accepts a reservation only when `used + qty <= limit`, otherwise it rejects the request and leaves the state untouched. Because rejection is a no-op, `used` can never cross `limit`, which is precisely the invariant the harness checks after every operation.

This is the deterministic core you would later lift into a property test. `invariant_holds` walks a fixed operation sequence and returns false the moment `used` exceeds `limit`; here it runs against five hand-picked scenarios with limit 8. Each scenario is constructed so that the checked reservation logic keeps the running total within bounds — the over-budget request in a scenario like [5, 4] is rejected rather than applied — so every case is valid.

`all_valid` folds `invariant_holds` over the scenarios with `all`, yielding true, and `violations` counts the scenarios where the invariant fails, yielding 0. The program prints the scenario count (5), the conjunction (true), and the violation count (0), matching the expected output exactly. Swapping the explicit list for a generated sequence and the `for` loop for a proptest body is the small step from this fixed-example harness to a real property test.

reviewAnswers.question: Why is a property test often a better fit than several ad hoc example tests for one invariant?
reviewAnswers.answer: An invariant is a rule that must hold across an entire space of inputs, and a handful of hand-picked examples only proves it for the cases someone happened to think of. A property test states the rule once and lets the framework generate hundreds of cases trying to break it, covering interleavings no human would write. When it does fail, shrinking reduces the counterexample to the smallest input that still violates the rule, so you get a pinpointed diagnosis instead of a vague failing fixture. The example tests grow linearly with effort; the property scales with the generator.

reviewAnswers.question: What does fuzzing prove that a curated integration fixture set usually does not prove?
reviewAnswers.answer: Fixtures prove that a few known, mostly well-formed inputs decode correctly; fuzzing proves the code survives the adversarial, malformed input space a human author would never enumerate. A coverage-guided fuzzer mutates bytes to reach new branches and surfaces crashes, panics, out-of-bounds reads, and undefined behavior in parsers and unsafe byte walkers. That is exactly where external input crosses into your code, and it is the class of failure fixtures miss because they are written from the perspective of valid data.

reviewAnswers.question: Why are sleep-based async tests brittle even when they 'usually pass' locally?
reviewAnswers.answer: A real sleep ties the test to wall-clock time and the scheduler, so it is really asserting 'this finished within N milliseconds on this machine' rather than the behavior you care about. That passes on a fast laptop and flakes on a loaded CI runner, because the margin depends on luck rather than logic. The fix is to take time out of the operating system's hands — pause the runtime and advance a fake clock explicitly past each deadline — so the test is deterministic regardless of machine speed.

reviewAnswers.question: What is the practical difference between golden files and snapshot tests?
reviewAnswers.answer: Both compare output against a stored artifact, but golden files are a strict, checked-in byte-for-byte reference suited to external contracts like wire frames or normalized CLI dumps, where any difference is a real change you must justify. Snapshot testing is the ergonomic cousin: a crate like insta captures output on first run and, on later runs, shows a diff and lets you accept or reject it with a review command, which fits human-reviewed, evolving output. The risk shared by both is that they prove the output looks like this, not that it is correct, so nondeterministic fields must be normalized and any load-bearing value needs a separate semantic assertion.

reviewAnswers.question: Why should benchmark regression budgets be looser and more isolated than ordinary correctness assertions?
reviewAnswers.answer: Benchmarks are inherently less deterministic than correctness tests — they are sensitive to hardware, build profile, and background load — so an exact timing assertion would flake constantly and erode trust in the suite. A coarse budget tied to a real product threshold (for example p95 under a stated microsecond bound) guards against meaningful regressions without failing on normal variance. Keeping them in a separate lane, often marked #[ignore], stops their noise from contaminating the fast, deterministic correctness run and keeps each layer proving the kind of claim it is good at.
